title: Autoregressive Language Modeling (Decoder-Only)
oneLineScope: Decoder-only, left-to-right language modeling: the GPT lineage and its causal factorization.
prose:
Where we are. The full transformer node left us with a two-part machine: an encoder that reads the source sentence with bidirectional attention, and a decoder that generates the target one token at a time while attending back to the encoder. That architecture was designed for translation — a task where you always have a complete source to condition on. Strip that requirement away. Suppose the task is simply to model language itself: to learn a probability distribution over sequences of text, with nothing as input except the text so far. The encoder becomes vestigial; the cross-attention sublayer has nothing to cross-attend to. This node is about what remains when you make that simplification, and why the result became the foundation of the GPT lineage.

The gist, in one paragraph. A decoder-only transformer is a stack of transformer blocks, each containing causal self-attention and a feed-forward network, with no encoder and no cross-attention. It models text strictly left to right: at each position it predicts the probability of the next token given all the preceding ones. The causal mask — the same above-diagonal zeroing introduced in the scaled-dot-product-attention node — is what enforces that left-to-right discipline inside the attention mechanism. Training minimizes the cross-entropy of the prediction at every position simultaneously, so the entire sequence contributes a learning signal in a single forward pass. At inference time the model generates one token, appends it to the input, and repeats — the autoregressive loop that names the approach.

Why it matters. This is not a simplification that sacrifices power: GPT-1, GPT-2, and their successors showed that a decoder-only transformer trained on enough text learns to transfer remarkably well to downstream tasks, and that at sufficient scale it begins adapting to new tasks from examples in the prompt alone. Understanding this architecture — what the causal mask does, how the training objective is connected to n-gram language models, why teacher forcing is used and what its cost is — is the prerequisite for understanding every large generative language model that followed.

The chain rule and its parameterization

A language model assigns a probability to a sequence of tokens. The oldest way to factor that probability is the chain rule of probability, applied left to right: write the joint distribution over a length-\(n\) sequence as a product of conditionals,

\[ p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) = \prod_{t=1}^{n} p(x_t \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{t-1}). \]

You know this factorization from n-gram models and from HMMs, where the Markov assumption was a device for making each conditional tractable. The question has always been how to parameterize \(p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) richly enough to capture long-range dependencies without an explosion in parameters. RNNs and LSTMs attacked this by threading a hidden state through the sequence, compressing history into a fixed-width vector at each step. The decoder-only transformer takes the opposite approach: abandon recurrence entirely, represent the whole prefix as a matrix, and use self-attention to let position \(t\) reach directly to any earlier position. The Markov truncation is gone; the only constraint is the causal mask that stops future tokens from leaking into the present.

The decoder-only architecture

Concretely: take the transformer from Vaswani et al., delete the encoder and the cross-attention sublayer in the decoder, and you have the decoder-only architecture. What remains is a stack of \(L\) identical blocks. Each block contains exactly two sublayers — causal self-attention and a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN) — each wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalization. The residual stream \(X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d_{\text{model}}}\), one row per token position, flows upward through all \(L\) blocks. At the top, a linear projection maps \(X\) to logits in \(\mathbb{R}^{n \times V}\) (one score per vocabulary entry per position), and a row-wise softmax turns each row into a probability distribution over the vocabulary. Position \(t\)’s output row is the model’s prediction \(p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t})\).

The right-shifted target alignment is how every position in the sequence contributes a loss simultaneously. The input to the model is tokens \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\); the target at position \(t\) is token \(x_{t+1}\). So the model’s output at position \(t\) is trained to predict the token at position \(t+1\) in the original sequence — the entire sequence’s worth of next-token predictions collapse into a single forward pass.

The causal mask is the mechanism

The left-to-right constraint is enforced entirely by the attention mask introduced in the scaled-dot-product-attention node. Recall that scaled dot-product attention forms an \(n \times n\) score matrix \(QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\), runs a row-wise softmax, and multiplies by \(V\). The causal mask sets every entry \((i, j)\) with \(j > i\) to \(-\infty\) before the softmax, which sends its exponential to exactly zero. Position \(t\) therefore receives contributions only from positions \(1, \ldots, t\) in the value-weighted mixture; it cannot see its own future.

This algebraic enforcement of order is what separates the decoder-only transformer from the old recurrent models. An LSTM could process only one step at a time because its hidden state literally depended on the previous step’s output. The causal transformer processes all \(n\) positions in a single parallel forward pass — every score in the \(n \times n\) matrix is computed simultaneously — and enforces the causal ordering by zeroing the upper triangle before the softmax. The information-flow constraint is real; the sequential computation cost is gone.

Training objective and teacher forcing

The model is trained to minimize the mean cross-entropy over all positions in all training sequences:

\[ \mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{t=1}^{n} \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_1, \ldots, x_{t-1}). \]

Here \(\theta\) collects all learnable parameters: the projection matrices \(W_Q, W_K, W_V, W_O\) in each attention layer, the FFN weights, the embedding matrix, and the output projection. The loss is computed against the gold tokens from the training data. This regime goes by the name teacher forcing: at training time the model always receives the correct prefix \(x_{<t}\), never its own previous predictions. Teacher forcing makes training stable and efficient — gradients are well-conditioned because the model never has to recover from its own earlier mistakes — but it introduces a train–test mismatch. At inference time there are no gold tokens; the model must condition on its own outputs, which may contain errors that compound. In information-theoretic terms, minimizing this loss is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence between the model’s next-token distribution and the true distribution of the training data, which is in turn equivalent to driving per-token perplexity toward the entropy of that distribution.

Autoregressive decoding at inference time

At inference time the teacher-forcing shortcut is gone. The model starts from a prompt (a prefix of tokens) and extends it one token at a time: run a forward pass over the current sequence, extract the distribution at the last position, sample or select a token, append it to the sequence, and repeat. This is the autoregressive loop — each new token feeds back as part of the context for the next step, hence the name.

Two selection rules dominate in practice. Greedy decoding always picks the argmax, \(\hat{x}_t = \arg\max_v \, p_\theta(v \mid x_{<t})\); it is deterministic but can loop or degenerate on long outputs. Sampling draws from the distribution directly, introducing stochasticity and typically producing more varied text. Nucleus (top-p) sampling, which restricts the draw to the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold \(p\), is the most common practical variant. These refinements are downstream of the core architecture.

GPT-1 and GPT-2: the recipe in practice

Radford et al. (2018) — GPT-1 — demonstrated that a decoder-only transformer pre-trained on large unlabeled text could be fine-tuned on downstream tasks with minimal task-specific changes. GPT-1 used \(L = 12\) decoder blocks, \(d_{\text{model}} = 768\), \(h = 12\) attention heads, and approximately 117 million parameters; training data was BooksCorpus (~800M words). The two-stage procedure — generative pre-training on the language modeling objective, then supervised fine-tuning on labeled data — was not new in spirit, but demonstrating it cleanly at this scale with a transformer was the contribution. The transfer learning framing echoes ELMo and ULMFiT, both of which also pre-trained a language model and then adapted it; GPT-1’s cleaner architecture and more uniform fine-tuning recipe made the approach easier to apply broadly.

GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) scaled the same recipe substantially: 48 layers, \(d_{\text{model}} = 1600\), up to 1.5 billion parameters for the largest variant, trained on WebText (~40 GB of web text filtered through Reddit upvotes). The architecture change was minor: layer normalization moved to the input of each sublayer (pre-norm rather than post-norm), a final layer normalization was added after the last block, and the context window extended to 1024 tokens. The finding was that, with enough data and compute, the same architecture and objective produced markedly more coherent long-form text. More striking was that a sufficiently large zero-shot GPT-2 was competitive with fine-tuned baselines on several NLP benchmarks without any task-specific training. That observation hinted at in-context learning — the model’s ability to adapt to a task from examples in the prompt alone — which the scaling-laws node and subsequent nodes in this graph take up.

What it cannot do by construction

An autoregressive language model has access only to left context at each position. That is exactly right for generation — you cannot condition a generative step on tokens you have not emitted yet — but it is a handicap for tasks where the answer depends on context from both directions: named-entity recognition, coreference resolution, reading comprehension where the relevant passage sits to the right of the question. For those tasks, conditioning only on the left half of the context is a structural limitation. The encoder-only approach of BERT addresses this directly, trading away generative capability in exchange for full bidirectional context; the masked-lm node describes that architecture and its training objective. The encoder-decoder-contrast node then maps out the tradeoffs among all three families side by side — the right place to settle “which architecture should I reach for?”

diagrams.caption: Decoder-only stack: input tokens flow through L causal-masked self-attention blocks, then a linear projection and softmax yield the next-token probability distribution.
diagrams.altText: A top-to-bottom stack. Input tokens (right-shifted) enter an embedding plus positional encoding layer, then pass through L decoder blocks each containing causal self-attention and an FFN. The top block feeds a linear projection to vocab size V, then a row-wise softmax producing the next-token distribution. A dashed annotation shows the right-shifted target: position t predicts token t+1. The cross-entropy loss is noted at the output.

An upward arrow leads to a box labeled 'embed + pos enc' with shape annotation 'X ∈ ℝⁿ ˣ ᵈmodel'. An upward arrow leads into a large box labeled 'decoder block × L'; inside the block, two inner boxes in sequence: 'causal self-attention (masked — no peeking right)' in red, then 'FFN' in black, connected by a rightward arrow. An ellipsis above the block indicates L blocks total. An upward arrow from the top of the block stack leads to a box labeled 'linear (n × V)' annotated 'projects to vocab logits'. A final upward arrow leads to a box labeled 'softmax → p(xₜ₊₁ | x₁…xₜ)' highlighted in green, with a shape note 'next-token distribution (n × V)'. On the right side, a dashed annotation reading 'target = input shifted left by one: position t predicts token t+1' with a leader arrow pointing toward the block stack. A second dashed annotation at the top reads 'loss: −Σ log p_θ(xₜ | x₁…xₜ₋₁)' pointing at the softmax output. Label every element; structural diagram.

diagrams.caption: The lower-triangular causal mask and the autoregressive feedback loop: each token sees only its own past, and each generated token becomes the next input.
diagrams.altText: Left panel: a 5-by-5 attention score matrix with the upper triangle shaded grey and labeled minus infinity, and the lower triangle plus diagonal shown as dots indicating allowed attention. The diagonal and below are accessible; above-diagonal entries are blocked. Right panel: an autoregressive decoding loop showing a prompt feeding into the model, which outputs a next token, which is appended to the prompt and fed back as input for the next step.

Row axis labeled 'query position (t)'; column axis labeled 'key position (j)'. A caption below reads 'causal mask: position t attends only to j ≤ t'. Right panel: an autoregressive feedback loop. bibliography.annotation: The GPT-1 paper. Introduces the decoder-only pre-training + fine-tuning recipe. See §3 for the architecture (12 layers, 117M params, BooksCorpus) and §3.2 for the training objective and teacher-forcing setup.

bibliography.citation: Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., & Sutskever, I. (2019). "Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners." OpenAI technical report.
bibliography.annotation: The GPT-2 paper. Scales the same decoder-only recipe to 1.5B parameters on WebText. §2 describes the architecture modifications (pre-norm, extended context). The zero-shot results that hint at in-context learning are in §3–4.
The clearest visual walkthrough of the decoder-only stack, the causal mask in attention, and the token-generation loop. Highly recommended as the first companion read after the GPT-2 paper's §2.

bibliography.citation: Karpathy, A. "Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code" (nanoGPT / Zero-to-Hero).
bibliography.annotation: Builds a decoder-only GPT in ~200 lines of PyTorch, making the causal mask, the training loop, and the autoregressive generation loop concrete. Ideal for seeing the architecture expressed as running code.
